The treasurer reports to every committee meeting on one sheet: the bank balance, the month's
income and spending against the budget, anything unusual, and anything the committee needs to
decide. The sheet is circulated two days before the meeting so that questions arrive before it rather
than during it, and it is filed with the minutes afterwards, where the examiner expects to find it and
where the next treasurer will look first.

Donations arrive a few times a year, usually from a former member or a family, and are
acknowledged by the chair in writing within the week, with the treasurer's note of how the money
will be used. A donation given for a purpose is spent on that purpose and reported back to the
donor when it has been; a donation given for the club in general goes to the boat fund unless the
committee decides otherwise at its next meeting, and that decision is minuted with the donor's
name, so that a future committee can see what was promised and to whom.

provenance.key:
Subscriptions fall due on the first of April and are the club's largest income. The rates are set at the
annual general meeting in March, published on the noticeboard and the website the same week, and
collected by the membership secretary, who passes the treasurer a list of who has paid every
fortnight until the end of May. A member who has not paid by the end of June is written to once,
kindly, and removed from the boat rota in July.

Concessions are offered to students, to members under twenty-five and to anyone who asks the
treasurer privately and has a reason, and the reason is not written down anywhere. The committee
approves the concession rates but not the individual concessions, which are the treasurer's call and
are reported only as a total. That arrangement has held for twenty years and has never been
abused, as far as anyone can tell.

The lease on the boathouse runs to 14 March 2019 and is reviewed by the harbour board every five
years, with the rent set at the review and paid quarterly in advance. The review letters, the signed
lease and the board's schedule of conditions are in the deed box at the bank, and the treasurer holds
copies. Anyone negotiating the next review should read the last three letters first, because the
board's position has not changed and neither has ours.

Insurance is renewed every October through the association's scheme, which covers the boats, the
boathouse contents, public liability and the committee's own liability. The schedule is checked
against the boat list before renewal, because a boat that has been sold is still being paid for until
somebody says so, and a boat that has been bought is not covered until somebody says so either.
The broker's letter goes in the October file.

The regatta in July is the club's second income and its largest single risk, because the costs are
committed in May and the entries arrive in June. The regatta secretary keeps a separate sheet for it,
agreed with the treasurer in April, and reports against it weekly from the first of June. A regatta that
is heading for a loss is cut back in June, not rescued in July, and the committee has learned to make
that decision early.

The bar is run by a rota of members under a licence held by the club, takes cards through the reader
on the counter, and banks its cash weekly. Stock is counted at the end of each month by two people
and the count is reconciled against sales by the treasurer. The bar is expected to make a small
surplus and is questioned if it does not, and the usual reason is a rota night that was not written up.

Grants are applied for by whoever has the energy, with the treasurer's figures and the chair's
signature, and are spent only on what the application said. A grant that arrives for a purpose the
club no longer needs is returned, with a letter, rather than quietly spent on something else; the club
has been funded twice by the same body because of that letter.
